title: Instead of getting recycled, many EV batteries are being repurposed
summary: As EV sales grew, many worried about what would happen to all those toxic batteries. Now, amid the demise of two big Canadian EV battery recyclers, another Canadian firm is building megafactories to…

image.caption: Sandra Aragon Aviles, battery systems engineer at Mapleview Energy, looks at a wall of mining vehicle batteries being repurposed as part of a pilot project at a farm in Elora, Ont., funded through the Ontario government's Ontario Vehicle Innovation Network. (Nick Nesbitt/Mapleview Energy)

blocks.text: As EV sales grew, many worried about what would happen to all those toxic batteries.
Recycling was once touted as a solution, but in the past two years, two major Canadian EV battery recyclers have gone bankrupt.
Meanwhile another Canadian firm, Moment Energy, is building megafactories to repurpose EV batteries for a surging industry — energy storage.
Here's a closer look at what's happening to EV batteries at the end of their lives as vehicle batteries.
Options for getting rid of an old EV battery
EV batteries are considered no longer suitable for driving after about a dozen years of use, when they reach about 80 per cent of their original capacity.
Automakers betting on EV rebate revival to turbo-charge sales
Federal and provincial regulations, which treat EV batteries as dangerous goods and hazardous waste or hazardous recyclable materials, effectively ban them from landfills.
That leaves two options: reuse and recycling.
Lithium battery recycling in Canada typically recovers metals such as nickel and copper, but burns off graphite and lithium, which make up half the battery.

Startups such as Quebec-based Lithion Technologies and Ontario-based Li-Cycle aimed to recover lithium and graphite (alongside the metals) through a new, high-tech process called hydrometallurgy. But both Li-Cycle and Lithion went bankrupt within the last two years.
Turning old electric vehicle batteries from trash to treasure

Maria Kelleher, a Toronto-based environmental consultant who has advised governments on what to do with old EV batteries, said the companies suffered from a lack of EV batteries to recycle. That was partly because EV batteries were lasting longer in vehicles than expected — 12 to 15 years instead of eight — and partly because an industry developed to reuse them.
"Recycling is what you would do when you can't do anything else with something," she said. "But reuse is much better."
How old EV batteries found a new life

According to the International Energy Agency, battery storage is the fastest-growing power technology in the world, with a 40 per cent jump in new capacity in 2025, to 108 gigawatts. In Canada, capacity doubled in 2025 to nearly a gigawatt and is expected to hit 15 to 23 GW by 2050, playing an "increasingly important role in providing system flexibility and reliability," according to the Canada Energy Regulator.
Amid slow electric vehicle market, NextStar prioritizes a different kind of battery

Surrey, B.C.-based Moment Energy tests and repackages old EV batteries for energy storage, marketing them at facilities such as factories, data centres and airports as a way to save on energy costs and help supply extra energy or backup power when needed.

Gurmesh Sidhu and three former classmates from Simon Fraser University's engineering program co-founded the company in 2019 after working in California, where EVs and solar panels were extremely popular.

They observed that recycling EV batteries was expensive. Meanwhile, there was a lot of solar power during the day, but that didn't match up with the need for EV charging and other power consumption at night.

The four co-founders of Moment Energy, Gabriel Soares (back-left), Gurmesh Sidhu (back-right), Sumreen Rattan (front-left) and Edward Chiang (front-right) showing models of their energy storage units inside the new Surrey, B.C., factory. (Moment Energy)
Sidhu said he believes "the only way to solve that sustainably is batteries."

Seven years later, this past June, the company officially opened what it believes to be the world's largest battery repurposing facility in Surrey, B.C. It's building an even bigger facility in Taylor, Texas, set to open next year, after raising more than $100 million US from investors. Last week, the company unveiled its newest, next-generation Nova battery made from repurposed EV batteries.
On Nov. 17, 2026, Moment Energy unveiled its newest, next-generation Nova battery made from repurposed EV batteries. (Moment Energy)
Meanwhile, other battery repurposing companies have been popping up in both Canada and the U.S.
Last week, one of the companies showcasing its technology at the MaRS Climate Impact Conference in Toronto was Ontario-based Mapleview Energy.

It's testing repurposed batteries from mining vehicles in a solar and battery storage system at a farm in Elora, Ont. Since the pilot launched this summer, it has cut the farm's power costs by 37 per cent, founder Nick Nesbitt said during a panel session.
The cost of a second life
Repurposing batteries also comes with costs and challenges.
Quebec based EVB360 developed a storage battery using refurbished Tesla Model 3 and Tesla Model Y batteries.

Martin Ménard, the company's director of project development, told CBC News in an email that the company recently decided to suspend its EV battery repurposing operations due to challenging market conditions.

blocks.text: In order to be repurposed, batteries from different brands with different chemistries and remaining capacities must be tested and evaluated. Special technology is needed for them to connect and work together safely. Then the system must undergo safety testing and certification.
It's something Moment Energy has successfully done, but it can be challenging for smaller companies. Ménard says it requires "significant investments."
Then there's the used battery supply problem.
An electric vehicle battery is displayed open during a demonstration at the EV & Charging Expo in Toronto in April. (Oksana Shtohryn/CBC)
Ménard recalled approaching automaker Stellantis about that. "I was told, 'Martin, come back and see us in 15 years' … There simply aren't enough end-of-life EV batteries available today."
Nesbitt acknowledges it's a challenge but believes it's solvable by tapping a wider range of EVs, from farming to mining to other industrial and delivery vehicles.

He added that repurposing companies can out-compete recyclers for batteries because their end product — stationary batteries — has a higher value than "black mass," the powdered mixture of metals and minerals produced by recyclers.

Ziyu Wang, a doctoral student at Concordia University in Montreal, did a study comparing recycling and repurposing EV batteries on Vancouver Island. In his study, he found that even regular recycling cost about $750 per EV battery, and hydrometallurgical recycling that recovers the lithium would cost about double that. Both are far from breaking even when the recovered materials are sold.
But even the cost of battery repurposing was higher than Wang thought it would be.

In all cases, Wang found transporting the heavy battery, which is regulated as hazardous waste, was a big component of the cost, as was evaluating the battery to see if it was suitable for repurposing or recycling.

He said these costs could be reduced by having more repurposing and recycling facilities. Regulations could also help, such as requiring "battery passports" that provide information about a battery's chemistry, history and state of health so less testing is needed. Such passports are being made mandatory in the European Union.
Meanwhile, given the increase in EV battery repurposing, economically feasible large-scale, advanced EV battery recycling may still be 10 to 30 years away, Kelleher estimates.
"We haven't gotten to the end of that life cycle."
